summary:
Sabah stands under the national framework of Malaysia. Sections 377A and 377B of the federal Penal Code 1936 criminalise "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" for any person regardless of gender or consent, with penalties of up to 20 years' imprisonment and whipping; these provisions are not limited to Malaysian citizens and reach foreign visitors. The Human Dignity Trust country profile for Malaysia, last updated 16 December 2025, further records that transgender people can be targeted through the "gross indecency" offence as well as through state Sharia enactments.

Every state, Sabah included, maintains a Sharia enactment prohibiting cross-dressing and "males posing as females", carrying penalties of up to three years' imprisonment. These state offences reach Muslims only, so a non-Muslim foreign visitor is not exposed to them; the federal Penal Code, by contrast, applies to everyone present in the country.

Enforcement against gender nonconformity is active. Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters, reporting on 10 August 2022, documented state-backed discrimination against LGBT people across the federation: arrests, criminal prosecutions at both the federal and state-Sharia level, and a crackdown that has persisted since the 2018 election. The Human Dignity Trust profile likewise reports arrests, prosecutions and corporal punishment under these provisions since 2018. The documented pattern is raid-based arrest and public exposure rather than individual stops against visitors.

The Nur Sajat case illustrates the machinery involved. In 2021 a transgender woman faced a religious-affairs arrest warrant and a search operation involving 122 officers. Both reports call for decriminalisation of same-sex conduct and gender diversity; no such reform has been enacted.

The audited sources for this record contain no Sabah-specific findings. Both the Human Dignity Trust profile and the Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters report address the national framework and federation-wide patterns, and state expressly that they carry no findings particular to Sabah. The assessment for Sabah therefore rests on the national legal position and the national enforcement pattern.

For a visitor, the practical exposure is the federal layer: arrest under the Penal Code remains possible in law, while enforcement against consenting adults in private is uncommon and tourists are rarely the target of individual stops. The acute documented risk arises from venue raids, where detainees are held, identified publicly and prosecuted.
tangentialFactors:
Litigation has narrowed the state layer without loosening the federal one. The High Court denied a request to declare the Sharia cross-dressing prohibition unconstitutional, and the Federal Court struck down Selangor's section 28 in February 2021 and 16 Kelantan Sharia provisions in February 2024 on federalism grounds, leaving the Penal Code offences fully intact. A constitutional challenge was pending as of late 2014 following the mass arrest of 16 trans women at a wedding on 8 June 2014.

Official hostility has been stated openly. In July 2020 the Religious Affairs Minister announced that the Federal Territories Islamic Religious Department (Jawi) had his "full licence to carry out its enforcement actions" against transgender persons, an order the International Commission of Jurists demanded be revoked. In the Nur Sajat case, 122 religious officers were mobilised to pursue her for "insulting Islam" before she fled to Thailand and received UNHCR protection.

Queue-and-venue raids carry acute exposure risk. On 28 November 2025 police raided a male-only sauna in Chow Kit, Kuala Lumpur, arresting 208 men under section 377B in the largest operation of its kind since 2022. Media were pre-tipped and detainees' faces and personal details were leaked; 17 civil servants identified among them were suspended. A magistrate rejected the remand extension as lacking ground, yet release was delayed, with more than 130 people held at one point including 31 foreign nationals whose embassies intervened. Justice For Sisters mobilised bailors and legal aid; on 2 December the Home Minister floated revisiting the provisions, and days later police raided another sauna in Penang.

Trans people in Malaysia face lethal violence and official indifference to it. A transgender woman was killed in Klang on 25 June 2019, the third killing of a trans woman in the country in fewer than two months; documentation of that case records police mistreatment and impunity under the heading "The Deceased Can't Speak for Herself".

The wider climate is one of state-backed restriction. Islamist opposition has foreclosed reform prospects, government-funded mukhayyam "rehabilitation" retreats had drawn 1,733 attendees by June 2021, and LGBT events and media content are censored. There is no same-sex marriage and no anti-discrimination law.
localsOnly:
The Sharia cross-dressing offences reach Muslims only, and enforcement is carried out by state Islamic religious departments. Since the 1980s all 13 states have passed such enactments, and three of them also bar women from posing as men. The laws contain no legal definition of what constitutes transgender dressing, which leaves the scope of the offence to the enforcing officer.

Residents who are Muslim face arrest, prosecution and caning under this layer, with penalties of up to three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning. Federal offences under Sections 377A and 377B apply to all residents regardless of religion, with a maximum of 20 years plus whipping.

Government-funded mukhayyam "rehabilitation" retreats had drawn 1,733 attendees by June 2021, and LGBT events and media content are censored. There is no same-sex marriage and no anti-discrimination law, and Islamist opposition has foreclosed reform prospects. Justice For Sisters has provided bailors and legal aid to those held in raids.
outOfScopeNotes:
The audited sources contain no Sabah-specific findings. Both the Human Dignity Trust profile and the Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters report address the national framework and federation-wide patterns only, so enforcement frequency, local religious-department practice and any Sabah-specific prosecutions remain unresolved on this record.

Legal gender recognition and document or marker rules for trans visitors are not addressed by the audited sources and remain unresolved here. Entry and visa screening that could expose a traveller's gender status, access to healthcare and hormone treatment in Sabah, and facilities or bathroom rules are likewise not sourced and should be treated as unverified.

The Human Dignity Trust profile was retrieved as a dated country profile (last updated 16 December 2025) rather than as a live enforcement log; the currency of its enforcement reporting after the 2018 election is not independently confirmed in this inventory.
